rules_text:
Rules summary Contents 1 OVERVIEW 2 ROUNDS 1 – 5 2.1 Deal Cards (4 cards total, according to the number of players): 2.2 Play Cards and Place Tiles 2.2.1 Card Order 2.2.2 Tile Placement Rules 3 ROUND 6 3.1 End of Round 4 Bonus Points OVERVIEW The game consists of 6 rounds. The player with the highest score after 6 rounds of scoring plus bonus points wins. ROUNDS 1 – 5 Deal Cards (4 cards total, according to the number of players): 1 Player Place 2 cards face up and 2 cards face down in front of you. 2 Players Deal 1 card to each player and place 1 card face down and 1 card face up in the center of the table. 3 Players Deal 1 Card to each player and place 1 card face up in the center of the table. 4 Players Deal 1 card to the player with the start marker, 1 card to the player to his or her left, 1 card to the remaining two players to share (both may look), and place 1 card face up in the center of the table. 5 Players Deal 1 card to the player with the start marker, 1 card to the two players to his or her right to share (both may look), 1 card to the two players to his or her left to share (both may look), and place 1 card face up in the center of the table. Play Cards and Place Tiles Starting with the face up card(s) on the table, each card is played one at a time. Players select the corresponding tile from their set and place it on their board. Every player places a tile for every card played (regardless of who plays it). After all cards have been played (and corresponding tiles placed), each player places one fountain tile (the single small triangle tiles). Card Order 1. Face Up Cards 2. Face Down Cards (applicable in 1 and 2 player games only) 3. Player with Start Marker’s Card 4. Continue clockwise until the rest of the cards are played Tile Placement Rules You May: · Place the tiles on empty squares · Rotate and flip the tiles before placing them · Place the tiles exclusively on your own City Board · Place tiles adjacent to and not adjacent to other tiles · Discard a tile rather than placing it You May Not: · Overlap or stack the tiles · Extend them beyond the edge of your City Board · Move them once the next card has been revealed · Play a tile that was previously discarded ROUND 6 Place the three remaining cards of the deck face up on the table. Players place their final three tiles simultaneously. Once all tiles are placed, each player places a final fountain tile. End of Round At the end of each round (including round 6, before assessing bonus points) you score points equal to the number of squares in your largest complete rectangle (for example, a rectangle of 3 x 4 would score 12 points). For end of round scoring, the tile color does not matter. Your red balance marker moves according to the number of squares in your city that are built with 2 red triangles. Your green balance marker moves according to green squares. Squares that are built with one red and one green triangle do not count for either color. Fountain tiles may count as either color when partnered with a red or green triangle, but not when partnered with another fountain tile. All cards used this round are discarded. The start marker moves to the player with the highest score (if tied, the start marker stops at the first tied player moving clockwise from its current position). Bonus Points After the final round end scoring and balance marker adjustments (following round 6), determine if any bonus points can be scored: Planning Bonus: 15 pts for a fully built 7x7 city board. Balance Bonus: Distance between red and green balance markers – 20 pts if no distance, 10 pts for 1-2, 5 pts for 3-4, 0 pts for 5+s for 1-2, 5 pts for 3-4, 0 pts for 5+

[Rating: 4/10] Even more than most Uwe games, this game just wants you to do as you are told, and unusually, what it tells you to do is the same every time. By the end of our second game we were filling the board perfectly and scoring within a margin of a few points on scores of over 200. I suspect it needs some other twist to trip people up or encourage variation.  [2 plays]

[Rating: 4/10] Not really a game. Not sure what I would call this but it's not really fun either

[Rating: 5/10] A tile laying game where you want to balance the number of green and red squares you create.  The game feels flat to me.  No need to own.

[Rating: 5/10] I think I just don't like Uwe Rosenberg games - does that make me a bad person? The polyominos are interesting because they are double-sided, and you want to balance your red and green squares by the end of the game. So that part of piecing everything together can be difficult and enjoyable. But at its core you are just laying tiles to build a relatively small city based on what this deck tells you to play. Not a ton of decisions or depth to the game in my opinion.

[Rating: 5/10] on n'est pas aux pièces !  Hey, j'ai une super idée ! Si je prenais un Tangram et que je lui ajoute un décompte de points ?! Génial Uwe ! Bon, tout est à peu près dit. Evidemment il y a beaucoup plus de pièces que dans le jeu original que l'on doit assembler sur une grille pour créer le rectangle parfait mais le fond reste le même. On tire une pièce et tous les joueurs doivent la placer sur leur grille. Aucune interaction, voilà un jeu solo dans toute sa splendeur. Si vous aimez les casse-tête à base de placement, n'hésitez pas à investir. Pour ceux qui désirent un moment ludique, ce n'est pas

[Rating: 5/10] MPS. So much counting. Awful score tracker. Card distribution system is just weird. But it's fun to fill your board and try to stay in balance.

[Rating: 5/10] Not an unenjoyable tile-laying puzzle, but a one that in an ocean of so many other tile-laying games goes very solidly into the bucket of “a game that exists”. The tangram shapes are less interesting / difficult to work with than it seems, and the whole idea about balancing two types of terrain is a complete wash.
